content: The Implementation Guide for the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use and Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use is a comprehensive document designed to assist countries in integrating the World Health Organization's (WHO) evidence-based recommendations into their national family planning guidelines. This guide is part of a global initiative to translate scientific guidance into practical application, using principles of implementation science. The WHO publishes two key guidelines for family planning service provision: 1. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC): This provides evidence-based guidance on the safety of various contraceptive methods in the context of specific health conditions and individual characteristics. 2. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR): This offers guidance on how to use contraceptive methods safely and effectively once they are deemed medically appropriate. These guidelines are intended to be used together to ensure comprehensive, evidence-based family planning services. The implementation of MEC and SPR guidance at the country level is critical for delivering high-quality family planning care. The guide emphasizes the importance of adapting the MEC and SPR recommendations to the national context while maintaining fidelity to the scientific content. Changes to the guidance should only be made in rare circumstances, such as when high-quality, country-specific data indicate the need for modifications. Any adaptations should be evidence-based and clearly documented, avoiding reliance on anecdotal, cultural, or social factors. The process of implementing MEC and SPR guidance involves a structured, multidisciplinary approach that engages multiple stakeholders. This includes ministries of health, national program managers, WHO country offices, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and other relevant partners. The guide provides practical tools and templates to support the adaptation and implementation of WHO recommendations into national programs, protocols, and service packages. Implementation science, as defined in the guide, is the study and application of methods to promote the adoption and integration of evidence-based policies, practices, and interventions into routine healthcare and public health settings. The implementation process is described as a dynamic and iterative process that includes four stages: 1. Exploration: Assessing the feasibility and relevance of the guidance. 2. Installation: Preparing the necessary infrastructure and resources for implementation. 3. Initial Implementation: Testing and refining the guidance in practice. 4. Full Implementation: Achieving sustainable integration of the guidance into routine practice. Implementation teams play a central role in this process. These teams, typically composed of 3–5 individuals with sufficient time and accountability, guide the process of change at each stage. Their responsibilities include completing activities, identifying barriers, ensuring the use of effective interventions, and applying evidence-based implementation strategies to achieve desired outcomes. The guide also highlights the importance of including all classes of family planning methods in national guidelines, even if certain methods are not currently available. This ensures that health systems are prepared to offer a full range of contraceptive options as availability changes over time. Adaptations at the national level provide valuable feedback for improving and updating global guidance. While WHO does not require approval of these adaptations, countries are encouraged to share them with WHO country and regional offices to inform future updates to global recommendations. The ultimate goals of the guide are: 1. To help countries take ownership of the guidance provided in the MEC and SPR. 2. To improve the usability of the guidance. 3. To translate policy into practice effectively. This guide was developed through a collaborative process involving international family planning experts, WHO staff, and stakeholders. It was supported by funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. The development process included consultations, working group meetings, and stakeholder reviews to ensure the guide's relevance and applicability to diverse settings.
